title: Victoria Harbour
wiki_lead:
Victoria Harbour is a natural landform harbour in Hong Kong separating Hong Kong Island to the south from the Kowloon Peninsula to the north. It is a major trading hub, as well as a tourist attraction. Lying in the middle of the territory's dense urban region, the harbour is also the site of annual fireworks displays and promenades.

The harbour has deep, sheltered waters and occupies a strategic location on the South China Sea, factors which were instrumental in Hong Kong's establishment as a British colony in 1841 and its subsequent development as a trading hub.
The harbour has seen numerous reclamation projects undertaken on both shores, many of which have caused controversy in recent years, including environmental concerns about water quality and loss of natural habitat. Land reclamation also narrows the width of the harbour, affecting the possible number of vessels passing through the harbour, though Victoria Harbour is still a port for thousands of international vessels each year.

Toponymy
The British colonial authorities who took control of Hong Kong in the 1840s initially referred to the harbour as "Hong Kong Harbour", but it was later renamed "Victoria Harbour", to assure shelter for the British fleet under Queen Victoria.


Extent
The plying limits of Victoria Harbour have been defined more than once by Hong Kong laws as follows:

"On the east-A straight line drawn from the westernmost extremity of Siu Chau Wan Point [小酒灣] to the westernmost extremity of A Kung Ngam Point (sometimes known as Kung Am);

On the west-A straight line drawn from the westernmost point of the Island of Hong Kong to the westernmost point of Green Island, thence a straight line drawn from the westernmost point of Green Island to the southeasternmost point of Tsing Yi, thence along the eastern and northern coast lines of Tsing Yi to the westernmost extremity of Tsing Yi and thence a straight line drawn true north therefrom to the mainland."


History

The first reference to what is now called Victoria Harbour is found in Zheng He's sailing maps of the China coast, dated c.1425, which appear in the Wubei Zhi (A Treatise on Armament Technology), a comprehensive 17th-century military book. While the harbour was charted in later maps, the first map depicting it in detail is an 1810 marine chart prepared for the East India Company by Daniel Ross and Philip Maughan, lieutenants of the Bombay Marine.
Some of the first recreational activities to take place in the harbour were water competitions such as swimming and water polo in the 1850s, undertaken by members of Hong Kong's first sports club, the Victoria Recreation Club.

During the Taiping Rebellion, armed rebels paraded the streets of Hong Kong. On 21 December 1854, the Hong Kong police arrested several armed rebels who were about to attack Kowloon City. grok_lead: Victoria Harbour is a natural deep-water harbour in Hong Kong, named after Queen Victoria following British colonial acquisition in 1841, that separates Hong Kong Island to the south from the Kowloon Peninsula to the north. Covering a surface area of 41.1 square kilometres, it features average depths of 12.2 metres and a maximum depth of 43 metres at Lei Yue Mun, providing sheltered access ideal for maritime activities. Its strategic location and geophysical advantagesâdeep, wide basins protected by surrounding hillsâmade it a cornerstone of Hong Kong's emergence as a global trade hub under British rule, facilitating the city's rapid industrialization and economic expansion in the 19th and 20th centuries. Throughout its history, Victoria Harbour has undergone extensive land reclamation to address Hong Kong's chronic land shortages amid population density exceeding 7 million residents, with projects dating back to the 1850s creating thousands of hectares for urban, commercial, and infrastructural development on both shores. These efforts, while enabling economic growth, have progressively narrowed the waterway, reducing its original expanse and prompting ongoing debates over diminished tidal flushing, water quality degradation, and loss of ecological function, as evidenced by environmental assessments highlighting risks to marine circulation. In recent years, legislative changes in 2025 have eased restrictions on further reclamation despite opposition from conservation advocates concerned with preserving the harbour's visual and functional integrity. Today, with container port operations largely relocated to deeper facilities at Kwai Tsing, Victoria Harbour functions primarily as a passenger and ferry terminal, cruise destination, and scenic focal point, underpinning tourism through attractions like waterfront promenades and the nightly Symphony of Lights display illuminating the adjacent skyscraper skyline. This transformation underscores its evolution from a utilitarian commercial asset to a cultural and aesthetic emblem of Hong Kong's vertical urbanism, where high-rise developments on reclaimed and natural land frame panoramic views symbolizing the territory's blend of geographical constraint and adaptive prosperity.
